skill.title: FastAPI
skill.summary: Request validation, dependency injection, response models and async handlers.
skill.description: Understand how FastAPI turns type hints into validation, how its dependency system resolves per request, and how async handlers interact with the event loop.

questions.title: A path parameter with the wrong type
questions.prompt: A client sends `GET /items/abc` to this endpoint. What response does FastAPI return?
questions.hint: FastAPI validates parameters against their type hints before your function runs.

options.text: `404 Not Found`, because no route matches `abc`
`422 Unprocessable Content` with a validation error for `item_id`
`500 Internal Server Error`, because `int("abc")` raises
`200 OK` with `item_id` set to the string `"abc"`

questions.explanation: The route matches; FastAPI then validates `item_id` against `int`. Validation fails before the handler is called, so FastAPI returns 422 with a JSON body describing which field failed and why.
rubric: Recognises that the route matches and validation happens afterwards.
Identifies 422 as FastAPI's validation error status.
Notes that the handler body never runs on invalid input.
misconceptions: Type hints in FastAPI are documentation only.
Invalid path parameters cause the route not to match.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Identifies a 422 validation error raised before the handler runs.

questions.title: Keeping secrets out of responses
questions.prompt: A handler returns a user object that includes `hashed_password`. Which approach reliably keeps that field out of the JSON response?

options.text: Declare `response_model=UserPublic`, a schema without `hashed_password`
Name the field `_hashed_password` so FastAPI treats it as private
Add a comment in the OpenAPI description telling clients to ignore it
Return the object unchanged; FastAPI never serialises fields named `password`

questions.explanation: FastAPI validates and filters the return value through `response_model`, so only fields declared on `UserPublic` are serialised. Separate input, storage and output schemas make leaks structurally impossible rather than relying on convention.
rubric: Chooses an explicit output schema via `response_model` or a return annotation.
Explains that FastAPI filters output to the declared fields.
Recommends separate schemas for input, storage and output.
misconceptions: Naming conventions hide fields from serialisation.
Frameworks automatically strip sensitive-looking fields.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Uses an explicit output schema (response_model or return type) so the field is never serialised.

questions.title: Shared sub-dependencies
questions.prompt: Both `get_current_user` and `get_repository` declare `Depends(get_db)`, and an endpoint depends on both. With default settings, how many times is `get_db` called for one request?
questions.hint: FastAPI keeps a per-request cache of dependency results.

options.text: Twice, once for each dependency that declares it
Once; the result is cached for the rest of that request
Once for the lifetime of the application
It depends on whether `get_db` is `async def`

questions.explanation: Within a single request FastAPI caches each dependency's result and reuses it for every dependant (`use_cache=True` by default). Both dependants therefore receive the same database session. Pass `Depends(get_db, use_cache=False)` if you genuinely need a fresh value.
rubric: States that dependency results are cached per request by default.
Distinguishes per-request caching from application-wide singletons.
Mentions `use_cache=False` as the opt-out.
misconceptions: Every `Depends` call executes the dependency again.
Dependencies are application-scoped singletons.

resources.title: FastAPI: Sub-dependencies (using the same dependency multiple times)

questions.acceptance_criteria: States get_db runs once per request because dependency results are cached per request.

questions.title: A blocking call inside `async def`
questions.prompt: This endpoint runs on a single Uvicorn worker. Under concurrent load, what is the effect of the `time.sleep` call?

options.text: Only this request waits two seconds; others are unaffected
FastAPI detects the blocking call and moves it to a thread pool
It blocks the event loop, stalling every request on that worker for two seconds
It raises an error because blocking calls are not allowed in coroutines

questions.explanation: `async def` handlers run directly on the event loop. A blocking call holds the loop, so no other request on that worker progresses. Use an async library (`await asyncio.sleep`, an async HTTP client), declare the handler with plain `def` so FastAPI runs it in a thread pool, or offload with `run_in_threadpool`.
rubric: Explains that `async def` handlers run on the event loop.
States that a blocking call stalls all concurrent requests on that worker.
Offers a fix: an async library, a plain `def` handler, or explicit thread offloading.
expected_concepts: `def` handlers run in a thread pool
misconceptions: `async def` makes any code inside it non-blocking.
FastAPI automatically offloads blocking calls made inside coroutines.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Explains the blocking call stalls the event loop for every request on the worker and gives a valid fix.

questions.title: Designing a database session dependency
questions.prompt: Design how a FastAPI service should create and provide async SQLAlchemy sessions. Cover where the engine is created and disposed, how a request gets its session, where transactions are committed or rolled back, and how tests can substitute a different database.
questions.hint: Distinguish objects that live for the whole application from objects that live for one request.
questions.explanation: Create the engine once per process (e.g. in a lifespan handler) because it owns the connection pool, and dispose it on shutdown. Provide one session per request through a `yield` dependency so cleanup runs after the response. Keep transaction boundaries explicit in the code that performs the unit of work, and roll back on error. Tests override the dependency or settings to point at a dedicated test database.
rubric: Creates the engine once per process and disposes it on shutdown, e.g. via lifespan.
Provides one session per request via a `yield` dependency that always closes it.
Defines clear transaction boundaries and rolls back on exceptions.
Explains how tests override the dependency or configuration to use a separate database.
Notes that engines and pooled connections must not be shared across event loops.
misconceptions: Creating a new engine per request is harmless.
A single global session can safely be shared between concurrent requests.
Commits happen automatically when the handler returns.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Creates the engine once per process, one session per request via a yield dependency, with explicit commit/rollback and a test override.

questions.title: Background tasks during a deploy
questions.prompt: A signup endpoint sends the welcome email with FastAPI's `BackgroundTasks`. During a rolling deploy, an instance is stopped seconds after returning the signup response. What happens to the email?
questions.hint: Where does the pending task live while it waits to run?

options.text: It is sent: FastAPI stores pending background tasks and resumes them on restart
It is sent: the response is held until all background tasks have finished
It may never be sent: tasks run in-process after the response and are not durable
It is sent by another instance: background tasks are shared across workers

questions.explanation: `BackgroundTasks` run in the same process after the response is sent. Nothing is persisted, retried or shared, so if the process stops first the work is lost silently. That is fine for best-effort work, but anything that must happen belongs in a durable queue (with retries and idempotency) processed by a worker, or in an outbox written in the request's transaction.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “It may never be sent: tasks run in-process after the response and are not durable”. `BackgroundTasks` run in the same process after the response is sent.
rubric: Explains that background tasks run in-process after the response.
Explains that they are lost if the process stops and are not retried.
Recommends a durable queue or outbox for must-happen work.
misconceptions: Background tasks survive restarts.
The client waits for background tasks.

questions.title: A PATCH that erases data
questions.prompt: Clients send partial updates such as `{"name": "Ada"}`. After this change, users who update only their name lose their email address. Why?
questions.hint: What does `model_dump()` return for a field the client never sent?

options.text: `model_dump()` includes every field, so unset fields overwrite stored values with `None`
Pydantic rejects partial bodies, so FastAPI fills missing fields from defaults
SQLAlchemy clears columns that are not passed to `setattr` in the same request
PATCH bodies are merged with the previous request's body by the HTTP client

questions.explanation: Every field on `UserPatch` defaults to `None`, so a body with only `name` produces `email=None`, and `model_dump()` includes it. The loop then writes `None` over the stored email. Use `model_dump(exclude_unset=True)` so only fields the client actually sent are applied. Keep in mind that `exclude_unset` distinguishes 'not sent' from 'sent as null', which matters if clients may clear a field deliberately.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “model_dump()` includes every field, so unset fields overwrite stored values with `None”. Every field on `UserPatch` defaults to `None`, so a body with only `name` produces `email=None`, and `model_dump()` includes it.
rubric: Identifies that defaults make omitted fields `None` in the dump.
Proposes `model_dump(exclude_unset=True)`.
Distinguishes a field that was not sent from one sent as null.
misconceptions: Missing fields in a request are ignored automatically.
`None` and 'not provided' mean the same thing.

resources.title: FastAPI docs: Body — updates (partial updates with exclude_unset)

questions.title: A request without a required query parameter
questions.prompt: A client calls `GET /search` with no query string. What does FastAPI return?
questions.hint: What makes a query parameter optional in FastAPI?

options.text: `200` with `q` set to `None`
`400 Bad Request` with an empty body
`422` with a JSON body describing the missing `q`
`500`, because the handler fails with a `TypeError`

questions.explanation: A parameter with a type annotation and no default is required. FastAPI validates the request before calling the handler, finds `q` missing, and responds with status 422 and a JSON `detail` list naming the location (`query`, `q`) and the error type. The handler never runs. Give `q` a default (for example `q: str | None = None`) to make it optional.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “422` with a JSON body describing the missing `q”. A parameter with a type annotation and no default is required.
rubric: Identifies `q` as required because it has no default.
States that FastAPI responds 422 before the handler runs.
Describes the error detail and how to make it optional.
misconceptions: Missing parameters become None automatically.
FastAPI returns 400 for validation errors by default.

questions.title: A test that still hits the real database
questions.prompt: A test uses `unittest.mock.patch("app.db.get_db", fake_get_db)`, but requests made with `TestClient` still use the real database. Endpoints declare `db = Depends(get_db)`. What is the right fix?
questions.hint: When did FastAPI capture the dependency function?

options.text: Patch `fastapi.Depends` so it returns the fake
Set `app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = fake_get_db` in the test
Call `fake_get_db()` at the top of every test before the request
Restart the app inside the test after applying the patch

questions.explanation: `Depends(get_db)` captured a reference to the original function object when the route was defined, so patching the module attribute later does not change what FastAPI calls. `app.dependency_overrides` maps the original dependency to a replacement and is consulted on every request, including sub-dependencies. Clear the overrides after the test (for example in a fixture) so tests stay isolated.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “Set `app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = fake_get_db` in the test”. `Depends(get_db)` captured a reference to the original function object when the route was defined, so patching the module attribute later does not change what FastAPI calls.
rubric: Explains that Depends holds a reference to the original function.
Uses `app.dependency_overrides`.
Resets overrides after the test.
misconceptions: Patching a module function changes every existing reference to it.
Dependencies are looked up by name at request time.

resources.title: FastAPI docs: Testing dependencies with overrides

questions.title: Moving blocking work to a plain def endpoint
questions.prompt: An endpoint calls a slow blocking SDK (about 2 seconds per call). It was `async def` and stalled every other request, so you changed it to plain `def`. Under 200 concurrent requests, other endpoints are fine but this one now queues heavily. Why?
questions.hint: How many worker threads can run `def` endpoints at the same time by default?

options.text: Plain `def` endpoints run one at a time on the event loop thread
Plain `def` endpoints run in a thread pool with a default limit of 40 threads
Uvicorn rejects concurrent connections to synchronous endpoints
Python's GIL blocks all threads while the SDK waits on the network

questions.explanation: FastAPI runs `def` endpoints in a worker thread so the event loop stays free. Those threads come from AnyIO's default capacity limiter, 40 tokens shared across the process, so at most about 40 of these calls run at once and the rest wait. Options: use an async client for the SDK, raise the limiter deliberately, run more worker processes, or move the slow call to a background queue. Blocking I/O releases the GIL, so the GIL is not the bottleneck.
questions.acceptance_criteria: Selects “Plain `def` endpoints run in a thread pool with a default limit of 40 threads”. FastAPI runs `def` endpoints in a worker thread so the event loop stays free.
rubric: Explains that `def` endpoints run in a thread pool.
Names the default limit of 40 threads.
Proposes an async client, a tuned limiter, more workers or a queue.
Explains why the GIL is not the cause.
misconceptions: Plain def endpoints block the event loop.
Threads waiting on the network hold the GIL.
